sections.title: FIN-M02-L02: Your net-worth statement
sections.summary: **Outcome:** List everything you own and owe at realistic values, calculate your net worth and liquid net worth with formulas, and set a date to update it. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Your **net worth** is a snapshot of your money on one day:

> **Net worth = everything you own (assets) − everything you owe (liabilities)**

It is the single best number for tracking progress over years. Income shows what flows in; net worth shows what you keep. Someone earning ₹80,000 a month with a car loan, a personal loan and card debt can have a lower net worth than someone earning ₹20,000 who saves steadily.

### What counts as an asset

- **Cash and bank:** cash at home, savings accounts, current accounts.
- **Deposits:** FDs, RDs (the amount paid in so far plus interest), post office schemes.
- **Retirement accounts:** EPF, GPF, PPF, NPS. You can't spend them now, but they are yours.
- **Investments:** mutual funds and shares at today's value (your consolidated account statement, or [CAS](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/cas.html), shows all your mutual funds in one place).
- **Gold:** weight × today's **buyback** rate (what a jeweller would pay you, which is lower than what you would pay to buy). In Kerala, gold is often counted in pavan: 1 pavan = 8 grams.
- **Property:** land or a house at a realistic sale value, from recent sales nearby, not the price you hope for.
- **Vehicles:** today's resale value, which falls every year.
- **Money owed to you:** only if you really expect it back.
- **Chitty:** for a chitty you haven't won yet, count the instalments you have paid; once you have taken the prize, the future instalments become a liability (FIN-M09-L07).

### What counts as a liability

Every loan's **outstanding principal** (not the total of future EMIs): home, vehicle, education, personal, gold loans; credit card balances; Buy Now Pay Later dues; money borrowed from family, friends or a chitty prize already taken.

### Liquid net worth

Much of a Kerala family's wealth is in land and gold, which can't pay a hospital bill tomorrow without a sale or a loan. So also track **liquid net worth**:

> **Liquid net worth = cash, bank and deposits you can withdraw within a week − short-term debts (cards, personal loans, BNPL)**

This tells you how prepared you are for a shock.

### Values: be honest and boring

Use conservative values. Overvaluing land and gold makes you feel rich and take risks you can't afford. When unsure, take the lower number. The point is the **trend**: update your net worth on the same date every month or quarter, using the same method each time.

### Negative net worth

If you owe more than you own, especially with an education loan, your net worth is negative. That is common early in life and is not a judgement. Track it anyway: watching a negative number shrink is one of the most motivating things in personal finance.

## Local example

**Rahul** made his first net-worth statement three months into his government job. (These numbers are made up, including the gold rate; use today's buyback rate for yours.)

| Asset | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Savings account balance | ₹18,000 |
| Fixed deposit | ₹25,000 |
| Gold jewellery, 3 pavan (24 g), at a made-up buyback rate | ₹2,16,000 |
| PF balance after the first months of service | ₹9,500 |
| Two-wheeler, resale value | ₹35,000 |
| Money lent to a cousin (likely to come back) | ₹10,000 |
| **Total assets** | **₹3,13,500** |

| Liability | Outstanding |
| --- | --- |
| Phone EMI, amount still owed | ₹21,000 |
| Credit card bill outstanding | ₹6,400 |
| Gold loan taken for his sister's admission | ₹60,000 |
| **Total liabilities** | **₹87,400** |

His **net worth** is ₹3,13,500 − ₹87,400 = **₹2,26,100**. Most of it is gold his mother gave him, which he doesn't intend to sell.

His **liquid net worth** is only the bank and FD (₹43,000) minus the card bill (₹6,400) = **₹36,600**. That surprised him: on paper he looked comfortable, but a ₹50,000 hospital bill would have meant another gold loan. It moved his emergency fund to the top of his goals list.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AMFI: consolidated account statement (CAS)](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/cas.html) | How to get a consolidated account statement of all your mutual funds by PAN (if you have any) | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | Any remaining part of the managing income and expenditure module; note how it lists assets and liabilities | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Net Worth** tab with the template headings.
2. List every asset with today's realistic value. For gold, weigh or check the bill for the weight, and find today's buyback rate from a jeweller. For land, ask what similar plots near you sold for.
3. List every liability with the outstanding principal. Your loan app or statement shows it; for cards, use the current balance; for family loans, the amount you owe.
4. Add the totals and formulas: total assets, total liabilities, net worth and liquid net worth.
5. Write the date at the top. Set a calendar reminder to update it on the same date next month.
6. Write two sentences: what surprised you, and which number you most want to change.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Net Worth tab with the date, totals, net worth and liquid net worth (cover any account numbers), and your two sentences, saved in 02 Goals.

## Template: Net Worth tab

```
Row 1: Item,Type (Asset/Liability),Category,Liquid? (Yes/No),Value (₹),How I valued it,Date
Rows 2-40: one row per asset or liability

Totals (put them in column H and I):
H2: Total assets        I2: =SUMIF(B2:B40,"Asset",E2:E40)
H3: Total liabilities   I3: =SUMIF(B2:B40,"Liability",E2:E40)
H4: Net worth           I4: =I2-I3
H5: Liquid assets       I5: =SUMIFS(E2:E40,B2:B40,"Asset",D2:D40,"Yes")
H6: Short-term debts    I6: =SUMIFS(E2:E40,B2:B40,"Liability",D2:D40,"Yes")
H7: Liquid net worth    I7: =I5-I6

Categories: Cash and bank / Deposits / Retirement / Investments / Gold / Property / Vehicle / Owed to me / Loan / Card / Family loan
For liabilities, "Liquid? Yes" means due within a year (cards, personal loans, BNPL).
```

## Template: net worth history (bottom of the tab or a new tab)

```csv
Date,Total assets,Total liabilities,Net worth,Liquid net worth,Change since last time,Note
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using the buying price of gold.** Use the buyback rate; after making charges and deductions, you get less than you paid.
- **Counting total future EMIs as the debt.** Use the outstanding principal from the lender's statement; future interest isn't owed yet.
- **Valuing land at a hoped-for price.** Use recent sales nearby, and the lower number when unsure.
- **Updating only when things look good.** Fix a date and stick to it; the trend is what matters.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is net worth?
    - A) The value of your house
    - B) Everything you own minus everything you owe
    - C) Your monthly salary
    - D) Your total income in a year
2. How should 3 pavan of gold jewellery be valued in a net-worth statement?
    - A) The price on the original bill
    - B) 24 grams × today's buyback rate
    - C) It shouldn't be counted
    - D) Today's selling price including making charges
3. Why track liquid net worth separately?
    - A) Land and gold can't pay an urgent bill without a sale or a loan
    - B) Banks require it
    - C) It decides your tax
    - D) It is always higher than net worth
4. For a loan, what goes in the liabilities list?
    - A) The total of all future EMIs
    - B) The outstanding principal
    - C) The original loan amount
    - D) Only the interest

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** How to get a consolidated mutual fund statement (CAS) and the NCFE module section on assets and liabilities
- **Action:** Build your dated Net Worth tab with realistic values, net worth and liquid net worth. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Net Worth tab with the date, totals, net worth and liquid net worth (cover any account numbers), and your two sentences, saved in 02 Goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** It is a snapshot of assets minus liabilities on one day.
2. **B.** 1 pavan is 8 grams, and the realistic value is what a jeweller would pay you today.
3. **A.** It shows how ready you are for a shock with money you can actually use this week.
4. **B.** The outstanding principal is what you would need to repay today to close it.

sections.title: FIN-M02-L03: Cash-flow statement and savings rate
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a monthly cash-flow statement from your log, calculate your savings rate, and see how irregular income behaves over several months. **Time:** about 2 hours (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 80 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Net worth is a photo; **cash flow** is a video. A cash-flow statement shows money coming in and going out over a period, usually a month:

> **Net cash flow = total money in − total money out**

If it is positive, you saved. If it is negative, you spent savings or borrowed. Over a year, positive cash flow is what makes net worth grow.

### Money in and money out

- **In:** salary after deductions, tuition or freelance fees, business profit you take home, interest, rent received, regular family support, gifts.
- **Out:** everything in your expense log: needs, wants, EMIs, family support you give, insurance premiums.
- **Not spending:** moving money to your own FD, RD or investments is **saving**, not an expense. Track it separately so your savings rate is honest.

### The savings rate

> **Savings rate = (money in − money spent) ÷ money in × 100**

It is the most useful single number for your progress, because it doesn't depend on how much you earn. A person earning ₹15,000 who saves ₹1,500 has a 10% savings rate; one earning ₹1,50,000 who saves ₹7,500 has only 5%. Many planners suggest aiming for **at least 20%** over time. If you are at 0% or below, getting to 5% is a real achievement. Raise it a little at a time, especially when income rises (the raise rule from Module 1).

### Irregular income: look at months, not one month

For freelancers, tutors, farmers and business owners, one month tells you little. Look at **the last six to twelve months**:

- **Average monthly income:** the total divided by the number of months
- **Lowest month:** your planning floor
- **Spending versus average income:** is the average enough?

FIN-M03-L04 turns this into a budget that survives slow months.

### Pulling numbers from your log with formulas

Your Expenses tab already has dates. **SUMIFS** adds amounts between two dates, so each month's spending fills itself in:

```
=SUMIFS(Expenses!B2:B500,Expenses!A2:A500,">="&DATE(2026,11,1),Expenses!A2:A500,"<"&DATE(2026,12,1))
```

This means: add column B in the Expenses tab where the date in column A is on or after 1 November 2026 and before 1 December 2026. It works in Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc (use semicolons in LibreOffice if your settings need them). In LibreOffice, a reference to another sheet is written `$Expenses.B2:B500`; if the `Expenses!` form shows an error, click the cells instead of typing the reference.

### What a cash-flow statement tells you

- **Where money leaks:** categories that grew without a decision
- **Seasons:** in Kerala, Onam, Vishu, school reopening in June, weddings and the monsoon often bring higher spending; plan for them
- **Whether a goal is realistic:** the monthly saving from your Goals tab must fit your real net cash flow, not your hoped-for one

## Local example

**Fathima's** freelance income over six months (made-up numbers):

| Month | Money in | Money out | Net cash flow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| May | ₹41,000 | ₹22,000 | ₹19,000 |
| June | ₹12,000 | ₹19,500 | -₹7,500 |
| July | ₹26,000 | ₹21,000 | ₹5,000 |
| August | ₹55,000 | ₹24,500 | ₹30,500 |
| September | ₹18,000 | ₹20,000 | -₹2,000 |
| October | ₹40,000 | ₹23,000 | ₹17,000 |

Her average income is ₹32,000 a month and her average spending ₹21,667, so her **average savings rate is about 32%**, which is healthy. But June and September were negative: she spent more than she earned and took the gap from savings. Her lowest month was ₹12,000, well below her spending.

Two lessons for her: the savings rate looks good **on average**, but she needs a buffer for slow months (FIN-M03-L04), and she needs to set aside tax from the big months (FIN-M10-L05). Seeing June and September side by side also showed her that two clients paid late in those months; she now asks for 50% in advance (pricing and terms are covered in the Entrepreneurship course, ENT-M05-L03).

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | Revise the managing income and expenditure module; then try one of the site's financial calculators | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 3, "Economic Foundations: Money and Rates": skim the opening section on money and interest rates | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Cash Flow** tab with the template headings, one row per month.
2. Fill in this month (or the days logged so far) from your Expenses tab using the SUMIFS formula. Add income from your bank statement or notes.
3. Go back as many months as you can (up to six) using your bank statements and UPI history for money in and out. Rough is fine for old months.
4. Add the savings rate formula and the averages at the bottom.
5. Compare your average monthly saving with the total monthly saving your Goals tab needs. Write down the gap.
6. Mark the months that were unusual (festivals, functions, fees) and note why.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Cash Flow tab with at least one full month (or your logged days so far), the savings rate formula and the gap between your goals and your real saving, saved in 02 Goals.

## Template: Cash Flow tab

```
Row 1: Month,Start date,End date,Income: salary or main,Income: other,Total in,Needs,Wants,EMIs and debt,Total spent,Saved or invested,Net cash flow,Savings rate %,Note
Row 2 example formulas (month starting in B2, ending before C2):
F2: =D2+E2
G2: =SUMIFS(Expenses!B2:B500,Expenses!A2:A500,">="&B2,Expenses!A2:A500,"<"&C2,Expenses!D2:D500,"Need")
H2: =SUMIFS(Expenses!B2:B500,Expenses!A2:A500,">="&B2,Expenses!A2:A500,"<"&C2,Expenses!D2:D500,"Want")
J2: =G2+H2+I2
L2: =F2-J2
M2: =IF(F2>0,L2/F2*100,0)
Averages (below the last month, for example row 14):
F14: =AVERAGE(F2:F13)    J14: =AVERAGE(J2:J13)    M14: =IF(F14>0,(F14-J14)/F14*100,0)
Lowest month of income: =MIN(F2:F13)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Counting savings transfers as spending.** Moving money to your RD or emergency fund is saving. Keep it out of "spent", or your savings rate looks worse than it is.
- **Judging irregular income by one month.** Use six to twelve months and plan on the lowest month, not the best.
- **Forgetting yearly costs.** Insurance premiums, school fees and festival spending hit one month hard. Spread them with sinking funds (Module 3).
- **Leaving out cash.** Cash spending is easy to forget and often the biggest leak. Your log must include it.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Income ₹25,000, spending ₹21,250. What is the savings rate?
    - A) 3.75%
    - B) 25%
    - C) 15%
    - D) 85%
2. You move ₹2,000 into your recurring deposit. In the cash-flow statement it is…
    - A) Saving, not spending
    - B) A want
    - C) Income
    - D) A need
3. For irregular income, what should a budget be built on?
    - A) Last month only
    - B) The best month
    - C) What you hope to earn
    - D) Several months of data, planning on the lowest month
4. What does SUMIFS add in the course formula?
    - A) Only the largest amount
    - B) Amounts whose dates fall between two dates
    - C) The number of rows
    - D) All amounts in the sheet

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The NCFE income and expenditure module (revision), one NCFE calculator and OpenStax chapter 3's opening section
- **Action:** Build a Cash Flow tab with your real months, savings rate and the gap to your goals. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Cash Flow tab with at least one full month (or your logged days so far), the savings rate formula and the gap between your goals and your real saving, saved in 02 Goals.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** (25,000 − 21,250) ÷ 25,000 × 100 = 15%.
2. **A.** It is still your money, just in another place.
3. **D.** Slow months come; plans built on the best month fail.
4. **B.** SUMIFS adds values that meet several conditions, here a start and an end date.

sections.title: Module 3: Budgeting
sections.summary: Turn your 30-day log into a budget you will actually keep: a method that fits you, a formula-driven sheet, sinking funds for yearly costs, and a system for irregular income.
sections.content:
## Overview

Your 30-day expense log ends in week 5. This module reads it, chooses a budgeting method that fits your income and personality, and builds a **Budget tab** that updates itself from the Expenses tab, with colour alerts when a category runs hot. Yearly costs such as insurance, fees and festivals become **sinking funds**, so they stop arriving as emergencies.

If your income is irregular, or will be (freelancing, tuition, a business), the last lesson gives you the salary system: a holding account, fixed splits for tax and costs, and a monthly salary to yourself. By the end of week 6 your budget system is running, and it becomes one of the eight parts of your final plan.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Summarise 30 days of spending by category with SUMIF and COUNTIF
- Choose and adapt 50/30/20, zero-based or envelope budgeting
- Plan sinking funds for yearly costs
- Build a Budget tab with planned vs actual, a zero check and colour alerts
- Run an irregular income through a holding account and a fixed monthly salary

## Time

About 9 hours in total: 8 hours of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 5–6.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M03-L01: Read your 30 days: where the money really went (about 2 hours)
2. FIN-M03-L02: Budget methods: 50/30/20, zero-based and envelopes (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
3. FIN-M03-L03: Your budget sheet: formulas, alerts and tools (about 2 hours 30 minutes)
4. FIN-M03-L04: Budgeting an irregular income (about 2 hours)

## Module project: My budget system

1. Write one page (or a note at the top of the Budget tab) describing your system: the method, your categories, your sinking funds, your pay-yourself-first transfer and, if relevant, your irregular-income salary.
2. Make sure next month's Budget tab is ready, with planned amounts that add up to your income.
3. Check that the standing instruction or RD for savings and sinking funds is set up.
4. Do one complete Sunday check and write what you changed.
5. At the end of the month, add a row to the Review tab: planned vs actual and one decision.

**Proof to record:** The one-page system description and a screenshot of next month's Budget tab with working formulas, saved in 03 Budget.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30-day data | Log incomplete | Log complete, not summarised | Summarised by category, with leaks and yearly costs listed |
| Method | None chosen | Chosen, not adapted | Chosen and adapted to your income, with a reason |
| Budget tab | No formulas | Some formulas | SUMIFS actuals, zero check and colour alerts all working |
| Automation | None | Planned, not set up | Pay-yourself-first and sinking funds set up |
| Irregular income | Not considered | Partly planned | Salary system planned (or ready for when income starts) |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Category summary of your 30 days with SUMIF (FIN-M03-L01, step 2).
- A 50/30/20 split of your income (FIN-M03-L02 template).
- One standing instruction for savings, even ₹200.
- A Budget tab with planned and actual for your three biggest categories only.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| 50/30/20 | 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payoff, adapted to your income. |
| Zero-based budget | Income minus every planned job, including savings, equals zero. |
| Envelope method | A fixed amount per category in cash or a separate account; when it's empty, spending stops. |
| Sinking fund | Monthly saving for a known yearly cost: yearly cost ÷ 12. |
| Pay yourself first | Move savings out the day income arrives, then live on the rest. |
| Holding account | For irregular income: everything comes in here, and you pay yourself a fixed salary from it. |
| Status formula | =IF(D4>C4,"OVER",IF(D4>0.8*C4,"Careful","OK")) |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **A budget that is never checked.** The weekly 10-minute check is the budget. Without it, the sheet is decoration.
- **A perfect budget in month one.** Expect two or three months of adjusting before the plan matches reality.
- **Treating yearly costs as emergencies.** Festivals, premiums and fees are certain. Sinking funds make them painless.

sections.title: FIN-M03-L01: Read your 30 days: where the money really went
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn your 30-day log into a category summary with formulas, find your three biggest leaks, and list the yearly costs a 30-day log misses. **Time:** about 2 hours (20 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 80 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Your 30-day log is finished (or nearly). It is the most honest picture of your money you have ever had. This lesson turns 30 days of rows into answers.

### Step 1: totals by category

A **category summary** adds up every category with one formula per row. In a new area of the Expenses tab (or a new tab called **Summary**), list your categories and use SUMIF:

```
=SUMIF(Expenses!C2:C500, A2, Expenses!B2:B500)
```

This means: in the Expenses tab, find rows where column C (category) matches the category written in A2, and add their amounts from column B. Add a **share** column (category ÷ total × 100) and a **count** column with COUNTIF to see how often you spend in each category.

### Step 2: three questions

1. **What are my three biggest categories?** These are where any real change happens. Cutting a ₹200 category by half saves ₹100; cutting a ₹3,000 category by a third saves ₹1,000.
2. **Where are the leaks?** A leak is frequent, small and unplanned: snacks, delivery, small app purchases, impulse UPI payments. COUNTIF finds them: a category with 40 payments a month is a habit, not an event.
3. **How far was my guess?** Compare the real total with the guess in your Baseline money snapshot. Most people underestimate by 20% or more. The gap is not a failure; it is why we log.

### Step 3: what 30 days misses

Some costs come once or twice a year, so a 30-day log may not show them. These are the costs that "suddenly" break budgets. List them now and divide each by 12 to get a monthly amount. Common ones in Kerala:

- Insurance premiums: health, vehicle, life
- School or college fees, books and uniforms when schools reopen in June
- Onam, Vishu, Christmas, Eid and other festival spending, including gifts and new clothes
- Weddings, house-warmings and other functions: gifts and travel
- Vehicle servicing, repairs and the yearly insurance renewal
- House repairs, often before or after the monsoon
- Property tax, annual subscriptions, gadget replacement

You will turn these into **sinking funds** in the next lesson: small monthly savings for known future bills.

### Step 4: a daily average

> **Daily average = 30-day total ÷ 30**

It is a simple number to watch in future months without a full log: if your average day costs ₹420, a ₹1,000 day stands out.

### What not to do with the results

Don't start cutting everything tomorrow. The goal of this lesson is to **see**. You decide what to change with a method in FIN-M03-L02, so the changes stick.

## Local example

**Anu's** 30 days, summarised with SUMIF (she earned about ₹14,000 that month):

| Category | Total | Share | Type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Food and groceries | ₹2,650 | 19% | Need |
| Eating out and snacks | ₹1,980 | 14% | Want |
| Transport and fuel | ₹1,120 | 8% | Need |
| Phone and internet | ₹399 | 3% | Need |
| Health and medicines | ₹860 | 6% | Need |
| Education and PSC | ₹1,240 | 9% | Need |
| Clothes and personal care | ₹1,450 | 10% | Want |
| Family support | ₹2,500 | 18% | Need |
| Gifts, functions and festivals | ₹1,000 | 7% | Want |
| Subscriptions and apps | ₹448 | 3% | Want |
| Other | ₹610 | 4% | Want |
| **Total** | **₹14,257** | 100% |  |

Her guess in week 0 had been ₹9,500; the real total was ₹14,257. Her wants came to ₹5,488, about 38% of spending.

Her three findings: **eating out and snacks** had 31 separate payments, almost all tea and snacks with friends after tuition, about ₹64 a day; **clothes** were one sale purchase (the earrings from Module 1) plus a kurta for a cousin's wedding; and the **subscriptions** were two video apps she rarely opened. Her yearly-costs list added another ₹1,850 a month: her share of the family health insurance premium, Onam, two weddings she already knew about, and her bus pass renewal.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | Revise the managing income and expenditure module and try the budget calculator if the site offers it | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Check the log is complete for 30 days. Fill gaps from your UPI history and note any days you are unsure about.
2. Build the category summary with the template formulas: total, share and count for each category.
3. Write your three biggest categories and your three biggest leaks.
4. Compare the 30-day total with your week 0 guess and write the difference in rupees and percent.
5. List every yearly or irregular cost you can think of, with its amount and month, and divide each by 12.
6. Calculate your daily average.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your category summary, your three biggest leaks, the guess-versus-real comparison and your yearly-costs list, saved in 03 Budget.

## Template: category summary (Summary tab, categories in A2:A16)

```
A: Category | B: Total (₹) | C: Share % | D: Number of payments | E: Average payment
B2: =SUMIF(Expenses!C$2:C$500,A2,Expenses!B$2:B$500)
C2: =IF(B$17>0,B2/B$17*100,0)
D2: =COUNTIF(Expenses!C$2:C$500,A2)
E2: =IF(D2>0,B2/D2,0)
Copy row 2 down to row 16.
B17: =SUM(B2:B16)          (total)
B18: =B17/30               (daily average)
B19: your week 0 guess     B20: =B17-B19 (difference)   B21: =IF(B19>0,B20/B19*100,0) (% off)
```

## Template: yearly costs list

```csv
Cost,Amount (₹),Month it comes,Monthly amount (=Amount/12)
Health insurance premium,,,
Vehicle insurance and service,,,
School or college fees and books,,,
Onam and other festivals,,,
Weddings and functions (gifts and travel),,,
House repairs,,,
Other,,,
Total monthly amount for sinking funds:,,,=SUM(D2:D8)
```

## Common mistakes

- **Judging the month as "good" or "bad".** It is data. The only bad log is an incomplete one.
- **Cutting small categories first.** Start with the biggest three; that is where real money is.
- **Forgetting yearly costs.** They are certain, just not monthly. Without sinking funds they arrive as "emergencies".
- **Category names typed differently.** "Food" and "food " (with a space) are different to SUMIF. Use the same words every time.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does =SUMIF(Expenses!C2:C500, A2, Expenses!B2:B500) do?
    - A) Adds amounts in column B where the category matches A2
    - B) Counts the number of rows
    - C) Adds all amounts in the sheet
    - D) Finds the largest amount
2. A category has 31 payments in 30 days, mostly small. What is it most likely to be?
    - A) A leak: a frequent, small habit worth looking at
    - B) A sinking fund
    - C) A one-time emergency
    - D) An investment
3. Why list yearly costs after a 30-day log?
    - A) They are always wants
    - B) They are tax-deductible
    - C) A 30-day log can miss bills that come once or twice a year
    - D) Banks require the list
4. Your 30 days total ₹12,600. What is your daily average?
    - A) ₹126
    - B) ₹42
    - C) ₹1,260
    - D) ₹420

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The NCFE income and expenditure module (revision) and its budget calculator
- **Action:** Summarise your 30-day log by category with formulas, find three leaks and list your yearly costs. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your category summary, your three biggest leaks, the guess-versus-real comparison and your yearly-costs list, saved in 03 Budget.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **A.** SUMIF adds the values whose category equals the one in A2.
2. **A.** High frequency of small, unplanned spends is the classic leak pattern.
3. **C.** Premiums, fees and festivals are certain but not monthly; dividing by 12 makes them plannable.
4. **D.** ₹12,600 ÷ 30 = ₹420.

sections.title: FIN-M03-L02: Budget methods: 50/30/20, zero-based and envelopes
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare the three main budgeting methods, adapt one to your income, and plan sinking funds for yearly costs. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 15 minutes resources, 50 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A budget is a **plan for money before it arrives**. Tracking (what you did in 30 days) looks back; budgeting looks forward. There are three main methods. All work; the best one is the one you will actually follow.

### Method 1: 50/30/20

Split take-home income into three buckets: **50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payoff**.

- **Good for:** beginners and steady incomes. Only three numbers to watch.
- **Adapt it:** on a small income, needs may take 60–70%. Then try **70/20/10** or **60/20/20** and move towards 20% savings as income grows. On a high income, try 40/20/40.
- **Watch out:** it hides detail. "Wants 30%" can still hide a leak.

**Worked example:** Rahul takes home ₹30,000. 50/30/20 gives needs ₹15,000, wants ₹9,000, savings ₹6,000. His real needs are ₹12,400 (Module 1), so needs are fine; his wants were ₹14,600 including the upgraded phone, so that bucket must shrink.

### Method 2: zero-based budget

Give **every rupee a job** until income minus all planned amounts equals zero. Savings and goals are jobs too.

> **Income − (needs + sinking funds + savings + debt payments + wants) = 0**

- **Good for:** tight budgets, people paying off debt, anyone who wants full control.
- **Watch out:** it takes 30–60 minutes a month to plan, and you must adjust when life changes. Keep a small "miscellaneous" line so one surprise doesn't break it.

### Method 3: envelopes

The traditional method: cash in labelled envelopes ("groceries ₹3,000", "bus ₹1,100"). When an envelope is empty, spending in that category stops. Today you can do this digitally:

- A **second savings account** or a separate pocket in your bank app for wants, so your main account holds only needs money
- **Recurring deposits** or a separate account for sinking funds, so festival money isn't spent in August
- Cash envelopes for the categories where you overspend most, such as snacks

- **Good for:** people whose leaks are in one or two categories, and households sharing money.
- **Watch out:** too many accounts become confusing. Two or three "envelopes" are enough.

### Pay yourself first, whichever method

On the day income arrives, move savings and sinking-fund money out **first**, using a standing instruction or a recurring deposit, and live on the rest. This one habit beats present bias (Module 1).

### Sinking funds: yearly costs, saved monthly

Take your yearly-costs list from FIN-M03-L01. Each item gets a monthly amount, saved into one separate account or RD. When Onam or the insurance renewal arrives, the money is waiting. Example: a ₹9,600 yearly health premium becomes ₹800 a month.

### Choosing

| If you… | Try |
| --- | --- |
| Want something simple and have steady income | 50/30/20, adapted to your income |
| Are paying off debt or living on a very tight income | Zero-based |
| Overspend in one or two categories | Envelopes for those categories, with 50/30/20 or zero-based for the rest |
| Have irregular income | Zero-based, using the method in FIN-M03-L04 |

## Local example

**Anu** chose a **zero-based budget with two envelopes**, because her income is small and irregular and her leaks were snacks and clothes. Her plan for a ₹14,000 month:

| Job | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Family support (to her mother on the 1st) | ₹2,500 |
| Needs: food share, bus, phone, medicines, PSC materials | ₹6,200 |
| Sinking funds RD (health premium share, Onam, weddings, bus pass) | ₹1,850 |
| Starter emergency fund (standing instruction on the 2nd) | ₹1,500 |
| Wants envelope: snacks and outings, in cash, ₹300 a week | ₹1,200 |
| Wants: clothes and personal care | ₹500 |
| Miscellaneous | ₹250 |
| **Total** | **₹14,000** |

Income minus jobs = ₹0. In a month when tuition brings in ₹18,000, the extra ₹4,000 goes to her emergency fund until it reaches its target. The cash envelope works because when the week's ₹300 is gone, she drinks tea at home, and she says she doesn't miss it as much as she expected.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The NCFE financial calculators: try the budget or savings calculator with your own numbers | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Read your category summary and yearly-costs list from FIN-M03-L01.
2. Choose one method (or a mix) using the table, and write one sentence on why it fits you.
3. Draft next month's plan on paper or in a note: every category with an amount, using your chosen method. For zero-based, income minus plan must be ₹0.
4. Set up your sinking-fund place: a recurring deposit or a separate account, and the monthly amount.
5. If you chose envelopes, set them up: cash envelopes or a second account for wants.
6. Set up one pay-yourself-first standing instruction for the day after income usually arrives (even ₹200 is fine to start).

**Proof to record:** Your written plan for next month (method, categories, amounts, total = income for zero-based) and a screenshot of the standing instruction or RD set up (cover account numbers), saved in 03 Budget.

## Template: 50/30/20 calculator

```
A2: take-home income (₹)
B2: needs %   (0.5, or 0.6 / 0.7 on a small income)
C2: wants %   (0.3 or 0.2)
D2: savings % =1-B2-C2
E2: needs ₹   =A2*B2
F2: wants ₹   =A2*C2
G2: savings ₹ =A2*D2
```

## Template: zero-based plan

```
Income this month: ₹____
1. Family support:          ₹____
2. Needs (list them):       ₹____
3. Debt payments:           ₹____
4. Sinking funds:           ₹____
5. Emergency fund / goals:  ₹____
6. Wants (with envelopes):  ₹____
7. Miscellaneous:           ₹____
Income minus all jobs = ₹0?  ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Copying 50/30/20 when needs are 65% of income.** Adapt the percentages to your reality, then improve them over time.
- **No wants in the budget.** A budget with no fun breaks in weeks. Plan your wants on purpose.
- **Saving "whatever is left".** Usually nothing is left. Pay yourself first, by standing instruction.
- **Too many envelopes.** Two or three envelopes are manageable; ten accounts become a mess.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Take-home income ₹30,000. Under 50/30/20, how much goes to savings and debt payoff?
    - A) ₹15,000
    - B) ₹3,000
    - C) ₹9,000
    - D) ₹6,000
2. What is the rule of a zero-based budget?
    - A) You spend nothing
    - B) You only track expenses
    - C) Income minus all planned jobs, including savings, equals zero
    - D) You save zero
3. A ₹9,600 yearly health premium as a sinking fund needs how much a month?
    - A) ₹96
    - B) ₹9,600
    - C) ₹960
    - D) ₹800
4. What does "pay yourself first" mean?
    - A) Buy yourself a gift every month
    - B) Pay your loans last
    - C) Spend first and save what is left
    - D) Move savings out on the day income arrives, then live on the rest

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The NCFE calculators, used with your own numbers
- **Action:** Choose a budget method, draft next month's plan and set up sinking funds and one pay-yourself-first transfer. It is done when your proof is saved: your written plan for next month (method, categories, amounts, total = income for zero-based) and a screenshot of the standing instruction or RD set up (cover account numbers), saved in 03 Budget.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **D.** 20% of ₹30,000 = ₹6,000.
2. **C.** Every rupee is given a job before the month starts.
3. **D.** ₹9,600 ÷ 12 = ₹800.
4. **D.** It puts saving before spending, so it actually happens.

sections.title: FIN-M03-L03: Your budget sheet: formulas, alerts and tools
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a Budget tab that compares planned and actual spending by formula, flags overspending automatically, and fits a 10-minute weekly check. **Time:** about 2 hours 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 100 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Your plan from FIN-M03-L02 becomes a **Budget tab** that fills itself in from the Expenses tab. You type each payment once in Expenses; the Budget tab does the adding.

### The layout

| Column | What it holds | Formula (row 4) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: Category | The same category names as the Expenses tab | (typed) |
| B: Type | Need, Want, Saving, Debt or Sinking | (typed) |
| C: Planned | This month's planned amount | (typed) |
| D: Actual | Spent this month so far | =SUMIFS(Expenses!$B$2:$B$1000,Expenses!$C$2:$C$1000,A4,Expenses!$A$2:$A$1000,">="&$B$1,Expenses!$A$2:$A$1000,"<"&$D$1) |
| E: Left | Planned minus actual | =C4-D4 |
| F: % used | How much of the plan is gone | =IF(C4>0,D4/C4*100,0) |
| G: Status | A word you can see at a glance | =IF(D4>C4,"OVER",IF(D4>0.8*C4,"Careful","OK")) |

Cell **B1** holds the first day of this month and **D1** the first day of next month, typed as `=DATE(2026,12,1)` and `=DATE(2027,1,1)`, so changing two dates resets the whole tab for a new month. The `$` signs keep ranges fixed when you copy the formula down.

### Totals and the zero check

- Total planned: `=SUM(C4:C20)`; total actual: `=SUM(D4:D20)`
- Income for the month in a cell, say C22, and the zero-based check: `=C22-SUM(C4:C20)` should show 0.
- Savings rate this month: `=SUMIF(B4:B20,"Saving",D4:D20)/C22*100`

### Colour alerts

Both Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc have **conditional formatting** (in the Format menu): make the Status cell red when it says OVER and orange for Careful. Colour gets your attention faster than numbers.

### The 10-minute weekly check

Every Sunday: log any missing payments, open the Budget tab, look at the Status column. For anything at "Careful", decide now: slow down, or move money from another category (in zero-based, a move keeps the total at zero). Don't wait for the month to end.

### Tools: what to use

- **Google Sheets** on the phone: the course's default; works offline once set up for offline use, syncs with the laptop.
- **[LibreOffice Calc](https://www.libreoffice.org/)** on the laptop: free and open source; opens .xlsx files. Remember the separator note in Week 0 ([formula options](https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/shared/optionen/01060900.html)).
- **[GnuCash](https://gnucash.org/)**: free, open-source double-entry accounting for Windows, macOS and Linux, with bank, investment and scheduled-transaction features. Useful later if your finances or freelance work grow complicated; overkill for most beginners.
- **Your bank app's spending analysis:** helpful for a quick look, but it can't see cash or other banks.
- **Budgeting apps that read your SMS:** some ask for permission to read all your messages, including bank alerts and OTPs. Think carefully before allowing that; this course doesn't need any such app.

### When a month goes over budget

It will happen. Ask: was the plan unrealistic (change the plan) or was it a one-off (absorb it from miscellaneous or wants)? Two months over in the same category means the plan is wrong, not you.

## Local example

**Rahul** built his Budget tab on his laptop in LibreOffice Calc, then moved it to Google Sheets so he could check it on his phone. His formulas showed an error in LibreOffice at first; changing the commas to semicolons fixed it, and Google Sheets accepted the commas again after he uploaded the file.

Mid-month, his Status column showed:

| Category | Planned | Actual | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Food and groceries | ₹4,000 | ₹2,150 | OK |
| Eating out and snacks | ₹2,000 | ₹1,780 | Careful |
| Clothes and personal care | ₹800 | ₹1,250 | OVER |
| Family support | ₹5,000 | ₹5,000 | Careful (fully paid, as planned) |

The OVER was a shirt for a colleague's wedding. He moved ₹450 from his miscellaneous line, and with "Careful" on eating out, he skipped one restaurant dinner that week. At month end he was within ₹200 of his plan, and he noticed the Sunday check took eight minutes.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [LibreOffice Help: formula options and separators](https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/shared/optionen/01060900.html) | Formula options: how LibreOffice separates the parts of a formula | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [GnuCash, free accounting software](https://gnucash.org/) | What GnuCash does, to know when you might need it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [LibreOffice (free office suite with Calc)](https://www.libreoffice.org/) | Download and install LibreOffice on the laptop if you want to work offline | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Budget** tab with the template. Type your categories and planned amounts from your plan in FIN-M03-L02.
2. Enter the month's first day in B1 and the next month's first day in D1. Copy the Actual, Left, % used and Status formulas down.
3. Add totals, the zero check and the savings rate formula.
4. Add conditional formatting so OVER shows red and Careful orange.
5. Test it: add a test payment in Expenses, check that Budget updates, then delete the test row.
6. Put a 10-minute weekly check in your calendar for every Sunday.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Budget tab with working formulas, totals and colour alerts for the current month, saved in 03 Budget.

## Template: Budget tab

```
A1: Month starts   B1: =DATE(2026,12,1)   C1: Next month starts   D1: =DATE(2027,1,1)
(Change the two dates each month. DATE avoids confusion between day/month orders.)
Row 3 headings: Category,Type,Planned,Actual,Left,% used,Status
Row 4 formulas (copy down to row 20):
D4: =SUMIFS(Expenses!$B$2:$B$1000,Expenses!$C$2:$C$1000,A4,Expenses!$A$2:$A$1000,">="&$B$1,Expenses!$A$2:$A$1000,"<"&$D$1)
E4: =C4-D4
F4: =IF(C4>0,D4/C4*100,0)
G4: =IF(D4>C4,"OVER",IF(D4>0.8*C4,"Careful","OK"))
Row 21: Totals   C21: =SUM(C4:C20)   D21: =SUM(D4:D20)
Row 22: Income this month   C22: (type it)
Row 23: Zero check          C23: =C22-C21
Row 24: Savings rate %      C24: =IF(C22>0,SUMIF(B4:B20,"Saving",D4:D20)/C22*100,0)
In LibreOffice: if a formula shows an error, use ; instead of , and click the other sheet's cells instead of typing Expenses!
```

## Template: weekly check

```
SUNDAY MONEY CHECK (10 minutes)
[ ] Log any missing payments (check UPI history and wallet)
[ ] Look at the Status column: any OVER or Careful?
[ ] Decide: slow down, or move money from: ____ to: ____
[ ] One sentence in the note: what I learned this week
```

## Common mistakes

- **Typing actual amounts by hand into the Budget tab.** Let SUMIFS do it from Expenses; typing twice creates errors.
- **Forgetting the $ signs.** Without them, ranges shift when you copy the formula down and totals go wrong.
- **Checking only at month end.** By then it is too late to change anything. The Sunday check is where budgets succeed.
- **Giving apps access to all your SMS.** Your messages include OTPs and bank alerts. A spreadsheet does the job without that risk.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why does the Budget tab use SUMIFS with dates in B1 and D1?
    - A) To calculate interest
    - B) To count categories
    - C) Because SUM doesn't work
    - D) So each month's actual spending is added automatically for each category
2. Planned ₹2,000, actual ₹1,780. What does the status formula show?
    - A) Careful
    - B) Error
    - C) OVER
    - D) OK
3. A formula copied from this course shows an error in LibreOffice. What should you try first?
    - A) Delete the sheet
    - B) Replace commas with semicolons
    - C) Switch off the laptop
    - D) Buy a budgeting app
4. What is the main risk of budgeting apps that read all your SMS?
    - A) They make spreadsheets slower
    - B) There is no risk
    - C) They change your tax regime
    - D) They can see bank alerts and OTPs

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** LibreOffice formula separators, the GnuCash overview and (optionally) installing LibreOffice
- **Action:** Build a Budget tab with SUMIFS formulas, totals, a zero check and colour alerts, and schedule the weekly check. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Budget tab with working formulas, totals and colour alerts for the current month, saved in 03 Budget.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **D.** SUMIFS adds a category's payments between the month's start and the next month's start.
2. **A.** ₹1,780 is more than 80% of ₹2,000 (₹1,600) but not over it.
3. **B.** LibreOffice may be set to use semicolons as separators.
4. **D.** Your messages hold sensitive financial information; share it only if you truly need to.

Action: Build a Budget tab with SUMIFS formulas, totals, a zero check and colour alerts, and schedule the weekly check

sections.title: FIN-M03-L04: Budgeting an irregular income
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a budget that survives slow months by paying yourself a fixed salary from a holding account, with tax and business money set aside from every payment. **Time:** about 2 hours (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 70 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Freelancers, tutors, commission agents, farmers, small shop owners and people waiting for their first job all face the same problem: **bills are regular, income isn't**. A normal budget breaks in the first slow month. This lesson gives you a system that works even if you have no income yet: you can set it up now and use it the day income starts.

### The core idea: pay yourself a salary

1. **All income goes into one holding account** (a separate savings account), never straight into spending.
2. **Every payment is split** the day it arrives: tax reserve, business costs, then the rest into holding.
3. **On the 1st of each month, you pay yourself a fixed "salary"** from holding to your spending account. The salary is your **baseline budget**: what you need to live on, based on your lowest normal month, not your best.
4. **When holding has more than 3 months of salary,** the extra goes to your goals.

Good months fill the holding account; slow months draw it down; your life sees the same salary either way.

### Step 1: the baseline budget

From your 30-day log and cash-flow history, list the **minimum** you need each month: needs, debt payments, sinking funds and a small amount for wants. This is the salary you pay yourself. If your average income is well above it, you can raise the salary later.

### Step 2: percentages for every payment

Decide fixed percentages so you don't think each time:

- **Tax reserve:** income tax isn't deducted from most freelance payments the way it is from a salary, and some clients deduct TDS (tax deducted at source) that you claim back when filing. Set aside a percentage until you calculate your real tax in Module 10. On a small income your tax may be zero under the new regime (FIN-M10-L02), but keep the habit.
- **Business costs:** software, data, travel, equipment.
- **GST:** if your turnover grows past the registration limit, GST you collect is not your money at all (FIN-M10-L05).

### Step 3: the buffer

The holding account needs a starting buffer. Aim for one month of salary first, then three. This **is not** your emergency fund (Module 5); the buffer covers normal slow months, the emergency fund covers shocks such as illness or a lost laptop.

### If income is seasonal

Tuition peaks before exams; some agriculture pays at harvest; tourism peaks in certain months. Look at 12 months of income, plan your salary on the yearly total ÷ 12 (minus a safety margin), and expect the holding account to rise and fall with the seasons.

### For a business

Keep business and personal money in separate accounts, and pay yourself a salary from business profit. Bookkeeping, profit and cash flow for a business are covered in the Entrepreneurship course (ENT-M08-L01 and ENT-M08-L02); this lesson covers your personal side.

## Local example

**Fathima's** lowest normal month in the last year was ₹12,000 and her average ₹32,000. Her baseline budget (needs, her loan EMI, sinking funds and modest wants) is ₹20,000. She opened a second savings account as her holding account.

When a client pays ₹45,000, she splits it the same day:

| Where | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Tax reserve (10%, an assumption until Module 10) | ₹4,500 |
| Business costs (software, internet share, 10%) | ₹4,500 |
| To the holding account (the rest) | ₹36,000 |

On the 1st of every month she transfers ₹20,000 from holding to her spending account. Over six months: her income varied from ₹12,000 to ₹55,000, but her spending account received ₹20,000 every month. By the sixth month the holding account held ₹38,000 above her salaries, almost two months of buffer. When it passes ₹60,000 (three months), the extra goes to her goals.

She found two side benefits: she stopped "celebrating" big payments with spending (mental accounting, Module 1), and at tax time the reserve was waiting.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Income-tax Act, 2025, section 58: presumptive taxation for small businesses and professionals](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-58-144) | Skim what "presumptive taxation" means for small businesses and professionals; you study it properly in FIN-M10-L05 | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [CBIC: registration under GST (PDF)](https://cbic-gst.gov.in/pdf/press-release/registrtn-gst-regime.pdf) | Read when GST registration becomes necessary, to know the limit exists | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | Revise the income and expenditure module with irregular income in mind | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. From your log and cash-flow history, calculate your baseline budget: the minimum monthly amount you need. Write the list.
2. Look at your income for as many months as you have. Write your lowest normal month and your average.
3. Choose your split percentages for each payment: tax reserve, business costs and holding.
4. Decide your holding account: a separate savings account (open one only if you have income to manage; otherwise write which account you would use).
5. Fill in the holding-account tracker in the template with your last three months, or with planned numbers if your income starts later.
6. Write your rule for extra money above three months of salary.
7. No income yet? Do steps 1, 3 and 6 with the income you expect from your first job or freelance work, and set a reminder to switch the plan on when the first payment arrives.

**Proof to record:** Your irregular-income plan (baseline budget, lowest and average income, split percentages, holding account and the tracker), saved in 03 Budget.

## Template: payment split calculator

```
A2: payment received (₹)
B2: tax reserve %          (e.g. 0.10)
C2: business costs %       (e.g. 0.10)
D2: tax reserve ₹          =A2*B2
E2: business costs ₹       =A2*C2
F2: to holding account ₹   =A2-D2-E2
```

## Template: holding account tracker

```csv
Month,Income received,Tax reserve,Business costs,Into holding,Salary paid to me,Holding balance,Months of buffer
(row 2) ,,,,=B2-C2-D2,,=E2-F2,=IF(F2>0,G2/F2,0)
(row 3) ,,,,=B3-C3-D3,,=G2+E3-F3,=IF(F3>0,G3/F3,0)
Rule: when months of buffer > 3, move the extra to: ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Budgeting on the best month.** Plan on the lowest normal month. Good months then become progress, not lifestyle.
- **Spending client money as it arrives.** Everything goes to holding first; your life runs on the salary.
- **No tax reserve.** Tax on a year's freelance income can be a shock in July. Set aside from every payment.
- **Mixing the buffer and the emergency fund.** The buffer smooths normal slow months; the emergency fund is for shocks. Keep both.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. In the salary system, where does all freelance income go first?
    - A) The spending account
    - B) Cash at home
    - C) A holding account
    - D) An investment
2. What should the monthly salary be based on?
    - A) Your baseline budget, from your lowest normal month
    - B) Last month's income
    - C) Your friend's income
    - D) Your best month
3. A ₹30,000 payment, with a 10% tax reserve and 10% business costs. How much goes to holding?
    - A) ₹21,000
    - B) ₹27,000
    - C) ₹30,000
    - D) ₹24,000
4. How is the buffer different from the emergency fund?
    - A) The buffer covers normal slow months; the emergency fund covers shocks
    - B) The buffer is invested in shares
    - C) They are the same
    - D) The emergency fund pays your tax

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The idea of presumptive taxation (section 58), when GST registration applies, and the NCFE income module
- **Action:** Write your irregular-income plan: baseline budget, split percentages, holding account and tracker. It is done when your proof is saved: your irregular-income plan (baseline budget, lowest and average income, split percentages, holding account and the tracker), saved in 03 Budget.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Holding receives everything; you pay yourself a fixed salary from it.
2. **A.** A salary you can pay even in slow months keeps the system stable.
3. **D.** ₹30,000 − ₹3,000 − ₹3,000 = ₹24,000.
4. **A.** Slow months are expected; illness or a lost laptop are shocks.

Action: Write your irregular-income plan: baseline budget, split percentages, holding account and tracker
tasks.detail: **Proof to record:** Your irregular-income plan (baseline budget, lowest and average income, split percentages, holding account and the tracker), saved in 03 Budget. Save it in your Money Folder and paste its link (or a short note of where it is) in this task's note. Never paste account numbers, passwords or OTPs anywhere.

sections.title: Module 4: Banking and payments
sections.summary: Clean up your bank accounts, make UPI and cards safe, know your rights after a fraud, and choose the right deposit for money you need soon.
sections.content:
## Overview

Banking is the plumbing of your money life. When it leaks, through charges, old phone numbers, missing nominees or a careless UPI approval, everything else suffers. This module audits every account you have, sets up safety habits for UPI, cards and net banking, and gives you a written plan for the first hour after a fraud.

The last lesson compares fixed deposits, recurring deposits and post office deposits on rate, safety, flexibility and tax, so your emergency fund (Module 5) and sinking funds (Module 3) have a sensible home.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- List and clean up every account you hold, including KYC, contacts and charges
- Explain deposit insurance and the ₹5 lakh per-bank limit
- Use UPI, cards and net banking with safe habits
- Explain your liability under RBI's rules and act within hours after a fraud
- Calculate FD and RD maturity values and choose where short-term money waits

## Time

About 6 hours 30 minutes in total: 5 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 7–8.

## Lessons

1. FIN-M04-L01: Bank accounts and KYC: the right account, kept clean (about 1 hour 30 minutes)
2. FIN-M04-L02: UPI, cards and net banking: using them safely (about 2 hours)
3. FIN-M04-L03: FDs, RDs and where to park money (about 2 hours)

## Module project: Bank and payments safety audit

1. Complete the Accounts tab: every account, type, contacts, nominee, KYC, charges and a keep/convert/close decision.
2. Score the 10-question payment safety check for yourself and one family member, and fix every "No" you can fix this week.
3. Put your fraud response card where you and your family can find it in a hurry.
4. Check the ₹5 lakh deposit insurance limit for every bank where you or your parents hold deposits.
5. Write a short summary: three things you fixed, and one thing still to do.

**Proof to record:** Accounts tab screenshot (last four digits only), the safety check scores before and after, and your summary, saved in 04 Banking.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts | Not listed | Listed without checks | Every account listed with contacts, nominee, KYC and charges checked |
| Clean-up | Nothing done | Planned | At least one action completed with proof |
| Payment safety | Alerts and controls off | Some set | Alerts on, card controls and limits set |
| Fraud plan | None | Card written | Card written, shared with family and easy to find |
| Deposits | Not compared | Rates noted | Compared on rate, safety, penalty and tax, with a decision |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- Turn on transaction alerts and card controls (FIN-M04-L02, steps 1 and 2).
- Write the fraud response card and tell your family about 1930.
- Check every account has your current mobile number.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer, then check. Repeat the ones you missed the next day.

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| DICGC deposit insurance limit | ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, principal plus interest (as of November 2026). |
| BSBD account | No minimum balance; free basic services, including at least four free withdrawals a month (digital payments not counted). |
| When do you need your UPI PIN? | Only to pay money out. Never to receive. |
| Third-party fraud reported within 3 working days | Zero liability for you. |
| The first call after a payment fraud | 1930, the national cyber crime helpline. |
| RBI Ombudsman | cms.rbi.org.in, free, after the bank rejects or doesn't reply in 30 days. |
| Cumulative FD formula | Deposit × (1 + rate ÷ 4) ^ (4 × years) for quarterly compounding. |
| Bank website addresses | End in .bank.in. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Treating safety as a one-time setup.** Revisit the safety check every year and whenever you get a new phone or number.
- **Chasing the highest deposit rate.** For short-term money, safety and access come first.
- **Keeping fraud knowledge to yourself.** Elderly parents and neighbours are targeted most. Share the card.

sections.title: FIN-M04-L01: Bank accounts and KYC: the right account, kept clean
sections.summary: **Outcome:** List every account you hold, know which type each one is and what it costs, and keep your KYC, contact details and deposit insurance limits in order. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Many people in Kerala have three or four bank accounts: one from school, one for a scholarship, one for salary, one at the co-operative bank near home. Some charge fees for low balances, some have old phone numbers, some have no nominee. This lesson cleans them up.

### Types of accounts

| Account | What it is for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Savings account | Everyday money; earns a little interest | Minimum balance rules and charges vary by bank |
| Basic savings bank deposit (BSBD) | A savings account with no minimum balance | Some limits on free withdrawals; see below |
| Salary account | Opened by your employer for salary credit | Its terms may change if salary stops coming; ask the bank |
| Current account | Business payments, many transactions | Usually no interest; higher balance rules |
| Joint account | Shared with a spouse or parent | How it can be operated after a death (Module 13) |
| Post office savings account | Small savings, linked to post office schemes | Interest 4% a year, as of November 2026 |

### The basic savings account (BSBD)

RBI expanded the free services of BSBD accounts in December 2025 ([Moneylife, December 2025](https://moneylife.in/article/rbi-expands-free-services-under-basic-savings-accounts-makes-switching-easier-for-customers/79041.html)): **no minimum balance and no initial deposit**; free deposits; **at least four free withdrawals a month**, with digital payments not counted in that limit; an ATM or debit card with no annual fee; 25 cheque leaves a year; internet and mobile banking; and a passbook or statement. You can ask your bank to **convert an existing savings account into a BSBD account**, which it must do within 7 days of your request. Check current rules with your bank.

If you keep a low balance and pay mostly by UPI, a BSBD account can end minimum-balance charges completely.

### KYC: Know Your Customer

Banks must verify who you are (identity) and where you live (address), usually with Aadhaar, PAN, a voter ID or a passport. Some points:

- **Re-KYC:** banks ask you to update KYC from time to time. A genuine request comes through your branch, the bank's official app or its official website, never through a link in an SMS from an unknown number.
- **Central KYC Registry (CKYC):** your KYC record can be shared between financial institutions, so you don't repeat it everywhere. RBI chose "KYC: Your First Step to Safe Banking" as the theme of Financial Literacy Week 2026 ([RBI Financial Education](https://rbi.org.in/financialeducation/)).
- **PAN** is needed for many transactions and for income tax; keep it linked to Aadhaar.
- **Your mobile number and email** must be current in every account. Fraud alerts and OTPs go there; an old number is a security hole.

### Deposit insurance: the ₹5 lakh rule

Deposits in banks are insured by the DICGC (a subsidiary of RBI) **up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including principal and interest** ([DICGC flyer](https://website.dicgc.org.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/DICGC_Flyer_0.pdf)). It covers commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, regional rural banks and co-operative banks registered with DICGC. If a bank fails, insured deposits are paid back up to that limit. Accounts in different branches of the same bank count together.

So **keep no more than about ₹5 lakh in any one bank**, counting all your accounts and FDs there, if safety matters to you. Co-operative **societies** that are not licensed banks are **not** covered by DICGC; RBI has warned that some of them wrongly use the word "bank" ([RBI, November 2021](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=52595)). Kerala has its own guarantee scheme for co-operative society deposits (FIN-M09-L07).

### Account hygiene

- Close accounts you don't need, after moving any balance and linked payments.
- An account with no transactions for a long time can become inoperative, and very old unclaimed balances are moved to an RBI fund; you can still claim them (FIN-M13-L02).
- Check the charges in your last six months of statements: SMS charges, minimum-balance penalties, card fees.

## Local example

**Anu** found four accounts in her name:

| Account | Status | Problem | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bank A savings, opened for a school scholarship | Active, old mobile number | ₹1,180 in minimum-balance charges over 6 months | Converted to BSBD at the branch; updated mobile number |
| Bank B savings, her main tuition account | Active | No nominee | Added a nominee (Module 13 explains the new rules) |
| Post office savings | Rarely used | None | Kept, for a future post office RD |
| Co-operative society deposit account her father opened | ₹4,000 | Not a licensed bank; no DICGC cover | Kept small; will review in FIN-M09-L07 |

The conversion took one visit and a written request. The bank's charges stopped from the next month, saving her more than ₹2,000 a year, which she moved straight into her emergency fund.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Moneylife: RBI expands free services in basic savings accounts (December 2025)](https://moneylife.in/article/rbi-expands-free-services-under-basic-savings-accounts-makes-switching-easier-for-customers/79041.html) | What a BSBD account must offer free, and the 7-day conversion rule | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [DICGC: deposit insurance, what is covered (PDF)](https://website.dicgc.org.in/sites/default/files/2024-09/DICGC_Flyer_0.pdf) | What deposit insurance covers, the ₹5 lakh limit and which banks are covered | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |
| [RBI: caution against co-operative societies using the word "bank" (November 2021)](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=52595) | Why some co-operative societies are not banks, and what that means for your deposit | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [RBI: Financial Education (messages, films, games, downloads)](https://rbi.org.in/financialeducation/) | The Financial Literacy Week 2026 KYC material in Downloads | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. List every account in your name: banks, post office, co-operative banks and societies, payments banks, wallets. Ask family if you are unsure about old accounts.
2. Make an **Accounts** tab with the template. Use only the last four digits of each account number.
3. For each account, check in the app or passbook: mobile number, email, nominee, KYC status and charges in the last six months.
4. Add up deposits in each bank to check the ₹5 lakh insurance limit (most people are far below it; note it anyway).
5. Choose one clean-up action and do it this week: convert to BSBD, update a mobile number, add a nominee, or start closing an unused account.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Accounts tab (last four digits only) and proof of one clean-up action, such as an acknowledgement or a screenshot of the updated details, saved in 04 Banking.

## Template: Accounts tab

```csv
Institution,Type (savings / BSBD / salary / current / joint / post office / co-op bank / co-op society / wallet),Last 4 digits,Insured by DICGC? (Yes/No/Check),Balance (₹),Mobile number current?,Email current?,Nominee?,KYC up to date?,Charges in last 6 months (₹),Keep / convert / close,Action date
```

## Template: formula: total in one bank (insurance check)

```
=SUMIF(A2:A20,"Bank A",E2:E20)     (add FDs in that bank too)
Over ₹5,00,000 in one bank? Consider spreading deposits.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring small charges.** ₹200 a month in penalties is ₹2,400 a year. Ask for a BSBD conversion or move to an account that suits your balance.
- **Old mobile numbers on accounts.** Fraud alerts go to that number. Update it in every account.
- **Updating KYC through an SMS link.** Use only the branch, the official app or the bank's own website.
- **Treating a co-operative society like a bank.** Not every society is a licensed bank, and DICGC cover depends on that. Check before depositing.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the DICGC deposit insurance limit, as of November 2026?
    - A) ₹1 lakh per account
    - B) ₹5 lakh per branch
    - C) Unlimited
    - D) ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including interest
2. Which is true of a BSBD account after RBI's December 2025 changes?
    - A) No ATM card allowed
    - B) A ₹10,000 minimum balance
    - C) No minimum balance, and at least four free withdrawals a month, not counting digital payments
    - D) No internet banking
3. You get an SMS: "Your KYC expires today, update here: [link]". What should you do?
    - A) Reply with your Aadhaar number
    - B) Forward it to friends
    - C) Ignore the link and check through the branch or official app
    - D) Click quickly before the account is blocked
4. Your deposit is in a co-operative credit society that isn't a licensed bank. Is it covered by DICGC?
    - A) Yes, up to ₹5 lakh
    - B) Yes, unlimited
    - C) No
    - D) Only the interest

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** BSBD rules, DICGC deposit insurance, RBI's caution on co-operative societies and the KYC material
- **Action:** Build your Accounts tab and complete one clean-up action. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Accounts tab (last four digits only) and proof of one clean-up action, such as an acknowledgement or a screenshot of the updated details, saved in 04 Banking.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **D.** It is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, with all branches of the bank counted together.
2. **C.** BSBD accounts must offer these basic services free.
3. **C.** Genuine KYC updates come through official channels; SMS links like this are a common fraud.
4. **C.** RBI has said DICGC cover is not available for deposits in such societies.
