sections.title: FIN-M08-L01: Inflation and compounding: the two forces on your money
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Calculate real returns, the future value of a lump sum and a SIP, and what a future amount is worth in today's rupees, in a Calculators tab. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Two forces act on every rupee you save: **inflation** quietly shrinks what it can buy, and **compounding** can make it grow. Investing is the art of making compounding beat inflation without taking risks you can't handle.

### Inflation

Inflation is the general rise in prices, measured in India mainly by the **consumer price index (CPI)**. The official target is **4%, within a band of 2% to 6%**, until March 2031 ([Outlook Money, March 2026](https://www.outlookmoney.com/banking/rbi-to-maintain-4-per-cent-inflation-target-until-2031-centre)). CPI inflation was **4.8% in August 2026**, and RBI raised its policy repo rate to 5.50% in October 2026 to keep prices in check ([SCC Online, October 2026](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/)).

At 5% inflation, something that costs ₹1,000 today costs about ₹1,629 in 10 years. Put the other way, **₹10,00,000 received 20 years from now buys only what about ₹3,76,889 buys today**:

> **Today's value of a future amount = future amount ÷ (1 + inflation) ^ years**

### Real return

The return that matters is what you earn **after** inflation:

> **Real return ≈ return − inflation** (exactly: (1 + return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1)

- Savings account at 3%, inflation at 5%: real return about **−1.9%**. The balance grows; its buying power shrinks.
- A deposit at 7%, inflation at 5%: real return about **+1.9%**, before tax on the interest.

Money for the next few years should be safe even if its real return is small. Money for 10 or 20 years needs a positive real return, or your goals keep running away from you.

### Compounding

Compounding means earning returns on your earlier returns:

> **Future value = amount today × (1 + yearly return) ^ years**

₹1,00,000 at 8% a year grows to about ₹2,15,892 in 10 years, ₹4,66,096 in 20 years and ₹10,06,266 in 30 years. The last 10 years add more than the first 20, because the base is bigger. **Time is the most powerful part of the formula.**

The **rule of 72** is a quick check: money doubles in about **72 ÷ return** years. At 8%, about 9 years; at 6%, about 12; at 12%, about 6.

### A SIP: investing every month

A **systematic investment plan (SIP)** puts in a fixed amount every month. The spreadsheet FV function gives the future value:

```
=FV(0.08/12, 33*12, -2000, 0, 1)
```

**Worked example:** starting at 27, ₹2,000 a month at an assumed 8% a year until 60 (33 years) grows to about **₹38,93,073**, from ₹7,92,000 paid in. Starting at 37 (23 years), it grows to only about **₹15,87,979**, from ₹5,52,000. To catch up, the late starter would need ₹4,000 a month, and would still end with about ₹31,75,957.

### A warning about assumed returns

Every number above uses an **assumed** return. Real investments don't grow at a steady 8%: some years they fall, some years they jump, and the average over your period is unknown in advance. Use calculators to understand the effect of time and amounts, not to promise yourself a result. When anyone shows you a calculator with a high return to sell you something, ask what happens in a bad decade (FIN-M08-L02).

## Local example

**Anu**, 27, and her friend **Sreeja**, 37, compared notes after a PSC class. Sreeja had saved nothing for retirement: "I'll start when I have a government job, with a bigger amount."

Anu put both of them into her new Calculators tab, at an assumed 8%: ₹2,000 a month from Anu's age until 60 gave about ₹38,93,073; the same amount from Sreeja's age gave about ₹15,87,979. Sreeja would need to put in twice as much each month just to come close.

Then they did the inflation step: at 5% inflation, Anu's ₹38,93,073 in 33 years would buy what about ₹7,78,118 buys today. "So the big number isn't as big as it looks," Sreeja said. "But starting late makes it much smaller." She started a small recurring deposit that week, planning to move it to a proper retirement plan after Module 12.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 3, "Economic Foundations: Money and Rates" (inflation and interest) and chapter 7 (future value): read the sections on inflation and compounding | 30 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Outlook Money: the 4% inflation target continues until 2031 (March 2026)](https://www.outlookmoney.com/banking/rbi-to-maintain-4-per-cent-inflation-target-until-2031-centre) | India's inflation target until 2031 | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SCC Online: RBI raises the repo rate to 5.50% (October 2026)](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/10/09/rbi-hikes-repo-rate-to-5-50-percent-october-2026/) | The October 2026 policy decision: repo rate and recent CPI inflation | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Make a **Calculators** tab with the template: lump-sum future value, SIP future value, today's value of a future amount, real return and the rule of 72.
2. Test each calculator with the worked examples from this lesson and check you get the same answers.
3. Calculate the real return on your own savings account and on one FD rate from Module 4, using 5% inflation.
4. Put your own numbers into the SIP calculator: the monthly amount you could invest, and the years until a long-term goal. Then try starting 5 years later.
5. Write two sentences: what surprised you, and what you will do differently.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your working Calculators tab with your own numbers and your two sentences, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: Calculators tab (labels in column A, inputs in B)

```
LUMP SUM
B2: amount today (₹)   B3: yearly return (e.g. 0.08)   B4: years
B5: future value   =B2*(1+B3)^B4

SIP (monthly, invested at the start of each month)
B8: monthly amount (₹)   B9: yearly return   B10: years
B11: future value  =FV(B9/12,B10*12,-B8,0,1)
B12: total paid    =B8*B10*12
B13: growth        =B11-B12

TODAY'S VALUE OF A FUTURE AMOUNT
B16: future amount (₹)   B17: inflation (e.g. 0.05)   B18: years
B19: in today's rupees  =B16/(1+B17)^B18

REAL RETURN
B22: return (e.g. 0.07)   B23: inflation (e.g. 0.05)
B24: real return %  =((1+B22)/(1+B23)-1)*100

RULE OF 72
B27: yearly return in % (e.g. 8)
B28: years to double, about  =72/B27
```

## Common mistakes

- **Ignoring inflation.** A goal 20 years away needs future rupees. Always convert both ways: future cost, and today's value of a future amount.
- **Treating an assumed return as a promise.** Calculators show the effect of time and amounts. Real returns vary year to year.
- **Waiting for a bigger income to start.** Time does more work than amount. Start small now and raise the amount later.
- **Keeping long-term money in a savings account.** A negative real return slowly eats it. Long-term money needs growth (FIN-M08-L03).

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. A deposit pays 7% and inflation is 5%. What is the real return, roughly?
    - A) −2%
    - B) 7%
    - C) About 2%
    - D) 12%
2. By the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
    - A) About 3 years
    - B) About 12 years
    - C) About 72 years
    - D) About 6 years
3. Which formula gives the future value of ₹2,000 a month for 20 years at 8%, invested at the start of each month?
    - A) =PMT(0.08, 20, 2000)
    - B) =2000*20*12
    - C) =FV(0.08/12, 20*12, -2000, 0, 1)
    - D) =2000*(1+0.08)^20
4. What is India's CPI inflation target for 2026 to 2031?
    - A) 4%, with a band of 2% to 6%
    - B) 0%
    - C) 10% to 12%
    - D) 8%
5. Why does starting 10 years earlier make such a big difference?
    - A) Inflation is lower for young people
    - B) Banks pay more to young people
    - C) Compounding has more years to work, and the last years add the most
    - D) It doesn't make a difference

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapters 3 and 7 on inflation and compounding, the inflation target and the October 2026 policy decision
- **Action:** Build a Calculators tab, test it, and run your own numbers for real return and a SIP. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your working Calculators tab with your own numbers and your two sentences, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **C.** Real return ≈ 7% − 5%; exactly (1.07 ÷ 1.05) − 1 ≈ 1.9%.
2. **B.** 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
3. **C.** FV with a monthly rate, the number of months, the payment and type 1.
4. **A.** The target was kept at 4% ± 2% until March 2031.
5. **C.** Time is the exponent in the compounding formula.

sections.title: FIN-M08-L02: Risk, return and the main asset classes
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain the main kinds of investment risk, describe each asset class honestly, and score your own risk profile. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Risk is more than "losing money"

| Risk | What it means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Market risk | Prices go up and down, sometimes a lot | Share prices fall sharply in a bad year |
| Inflation risk | Returns don't keep up with prices | A savings account at 3% when prices rise 5% |
| Credit (default) risk | The borrower doesn't pay you back | A company or society fails to repay a deposit or bond |
| Interest-rate risk | Bond and debt fund prices fall when rates rise | A long-term bond fund dips after a rate rise |
| Liquidity risk | You can't sell quickly at a fair price | Land that takes a year to sell |
| Concentration risk | Too much in one thing | All savings in one stock, one plot or one society |
| Fraud risk | The product or the seller is a scam | A "scheme" promising 5% a month (Module 15) |

There is no investment without risk; even "safe" deposits carry inflation risk.

### The main asset classes

| Asset class | Examples | Return potential | Main risks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cash and deposits | Savings, FDs, RDs | Low; may not beat inflation after tax | Inflation; credit risk above insurance limits |
| Debt (lending) | Government small savings, PPF, EPF, bonds, debt mutual funds | Low to moderate | Interest-rate and credit risk; government-backed schemes have very low credit risk |
| Equity (ownership) | Shares, equity mutual funds, index funds | Highest over long periods | Large falls in bad years; years to recover |
| Gold | Gold ETFs, gold mutual funds, jewellery | Varies; often rises when other assets fall | Long flat periods; jewellery has making charges and purity issues |
| Real estate | Land, a house, REITs | Varies by place | Illiquid, large amounts, legal issues, costs |
| Speculative | Crypto, derivatives (F&O) | Uncertain | Very high volatility; SEBI found about 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in 2024-25 ([Moneylife](https://moneylife.in/article/91-percentage-of-retail-traders-lost-money-in-derivatives-losses-in-fo-surged-41-percentage-to-rs105-lakh-crore-in-fy2425-sebi-study/77613.html)) |

### The risk–return trade-off

Higher possible returns come with higher risk. It never works the other way: **"high returns with no risk" doesn't exist**. When someone offers it, you are looking at a misunderstanding or a fraud.

Equity's long-term return potential is higher because investors are paid for living through its falls. If you will panic and sell in a fall, you get the falls without the long-term reward.

### The riskometer

Every mutual fund in India shows a **riskometer**, SEBI's standard risk scale with six levels: **Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High and Very High** ([AMFI](https://www.mutualfundssahihai.com/en/what-riskometer-and-what-are-different-levels)). It is based on the fund's holdings, volatility, and credit and interest-rate risk, and must appear in factsheets and promotional material ([SEBI investor site](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html)). You will use it to compare funds in FIN-M09-L02.

### Your risk profile: two different things

- **Risk capacity:** how much loss your finances can survive. A full emergency fund, stable income, insurance, no expensive debt and a long time horizon all raise it.
- **Risk tolerance:** how much loss you can live with emotionally without panicking.

Invest according to the **lower** of the two. A government employee with a pension may have high capacity but low tolerance; a young freelancer may feel brave but have low capacity.

### Time horizon changes everything

Money needed in 2 years can't wait for a market to recover; money needed in 20 years can. So the same person can have safe money for short goals and growth money for long ones. That is the idea behind asset allocation, in the next lesson.

## Local example

**Fathima** scored herself with the risk profile in this lesson. Her **tolerance** came out high: she enjoys reading about markets and wasn't worried by the idea of a 30% fall. But her **capacity** came out low: irregular income, an emergency fund only half built, and a two-wheeler loan.

Her conclusion: "My head says high risk, my situation says not yet." She decided that until her emergency fund was full and her loan cleared, new long-term money would go mostly to safer options, with only a small share in equity, rising once her capacity improved. She wrote the rule in her Calculators tab so she wouldn't change her mind after a good month in the markets.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [AMFI (Mutual Funds Sahi Hai): the six riskometer levels](https://www.mutualfundssahihai.com/en/what-riskometer-and-what-are-different-levels) | The six riskometer levels | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [SEBI investor website: riskometer](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html) | How the riskometer is decided and where you will see it | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Moneylife: SEBI study, 91% of individual F&O traders lost money in 2024-25](https://moneylife.in/article/91-percentage-of-retail-traders-lost-money-in-derivatives-losses-in-fo-surged-41-percentage-to-rs105-lakh-crore-in-fy2425-sebi-study/77613.html) | SEBI's study of losses in futures and options trading | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 15, "How to Think about Investing": read the opening sections on risk and return | 25 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. Answer the 10 risk-profile questions honestly and add up your capacity and tolerance scores.
2. Write your profile: the lower of the two scores decides it.
3. In your Goals tab, add a column "time horizon" and mark each goal short (under 3 years), medium (3 to 7) or long (over 7).
4. For each risk in the table, write one place it already exists in your family's money (for example, concentration: all savings in one co-op society).
5. Write one rule that follows from your profile, like Fathima's.

**Proof to record:** Your scored risk profile, the horizon column in your Goals tab and your one rule, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: risk profile (score each answer 1 to 3)

```
CAPACITY (what your finances can survive)
1. Emergency fund: none (1) / partly built (2) / full (3)
2. Income: irregular (1) / steady private job (2) / permanent or very secure (3)
3. Expensive debt (cards, personal loans): yes (1) / some (2) / none (3)
4. Health and life cover in place: no (1) / partly (2) / yes (3)
5. Years until you need this money: under 3 (1) / 3 to 7 (2) / over 7 (3)
Capacity score: ____ / 15

TOLERANCE (what you can live with)
6. If your investment fell 25% in a year, you would: sell everything (1) / wait, worried (2) / hold or add more (3)
7. You prefer: certain small growth (1) / some ups and downs (2) / big ups and downs for more growth (3)
8. You check investments: daily and worry (1) / monthly (2) / a few times a year (3)
9. Past loss experience: panicked (1) / no experience (2) / stayed calm (3)
10. Sleep test: losses would keep you awake (1) / sometimes (2) / no (3)
Tolerance score: ____ / 15

Profile = the LOWER score:  5-8 cautious   9-11 balanced   12-15 growth
```

## Common mistakes

- **Thinking deposits are risk-free.** They carry inflation risk, and credit risk above insurance limits or in unlicensed societies.
- **Judging risk by last year's returns.** A great year says nothing about the next one. Look at what can go wrong.
- **Investing by tolerance alone.** Courage doesn't pay bills in a crisis. Capacity decides too.
- **Believing "guaranteed high returns".** High return and no risk never come together. It is the first sign of a scam.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which risk does a savings account carry even though the balance never falls?
    - A) Market risk
    - B) Inflation risk
    - C) Liquidity risk
    - D) No risk at all
2. How many levels does SEBI's riskometer have?
    - A) Two
    - B) Three
    - C) Ten
    - D) Six
3. Your tolerance score is high but your capacity is low. What should decide your investments?
    - A) The higher one: tolerance
    - B) Last year's best fund
    - C) Whatever friends do
    - D) The lower one: capacity
4. What did SEBI's study find about individual F&O traders in 2024-25?
    - A) Most made steady profits
    - B) Half doubled their money
    - C) Nobody traded
    - D) About 91% lost money

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The riskometer (AMFI and SEBI), SEBI's F&O loss study and OpenStax chapter 15's opening sections
- **Action:** Score your risk profile, mark each goal's time horizon and write one rule. It is done when your proof is saved: your scored risk profile, the horizon column in your Goals tab and your one rule, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** If interest is below inflation, buying power shrinks.
2. **D.** Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High, Very High.
3. **D.** Invest by the lower of the two so a bad year doesn't break your plan.
4. **D.** Net losses were over ₹1 lakh crore in the year.

sections.title: FIN-M08-L03: Asset allocation, diversification and rebalancing
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Set a target asset allocation for your long-term money based on your goals and risk profile, and use a formula to know when to rebalance. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (25 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Asset allocation

**Asset allocation** is how you split your investments between asset classes: equity, debt, gold and cash. It matters more for your long-term result than which individual fund or stock you pick, because it decides how much your money can grow and how far it can fall.

### Allocation by goal

The simplest method follows the time horizons you marked in FIN-M08-L02:

| Goal horizon | Typical allocation | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 3 years | All safe: deposits, RDs, small savings, very low-risk debt | No time to recover from a fall |
| 3 to 7 years | Mostly safe, some equity (for example 20–40%) | Some growth, limited damage in a bad year |
| Over 7 years (retirement, a child's education) | More equity (for example 50–70%), the rest debt, perhaps some gold | Time to ride out falls; needs to beat inflation |

These are examples to think with, not recommendations. Adjust them for your risk profile: a cautious profile uses the lower equity numbers or less. One rule of thumb some people use for long-term money is "100 minus your age" in equity; treat it as a starting point for thinking, not an answer.

Remember money you already have in **EPF, GPF or PPF**: it is debt. If you are a government employee with GPF or NPS contributions (Module 14), count them in your allocation.

### Diversification

**Don't put all your eggs in one basket**, within and across asset classes:

- **Across classes:** equity, debt and gold rarely all fall at the same time.
- **Within a class:** one company's shares can go to zero; an index fund holding many companies is far less likely to. One co-operative society can fail; deposits spread across insured banks and government schemes are safer.
- **Kerala's common concentration:** most family wealth in one plot of land, one house and gold. Diversifying doesn't mean selling the house; it means new savings go elsewhere.

### Rebalancing

Over time, the assets that grew fastest become a bigger share than you planned. If equity rises, your portfolio becomes riskier without you deciding it. **Rebalancing** brings it back to target:

1. **Check once a year**, on a fixed date (your yearly review, FIN-M17-L03).
2. **Rebalance if any class has drifted more than 5 percentage points** from its target (your rule; some use 10).
3. **First, direct new money** to the asset class that is below target. This avoids selling.
4. **Only if needed, sell** some of what is above target and buy what is below, thinking about tax (Module 10) and exit loads.

**Worked example:** Rahul's target is 60% equity, 35% debt, 5% gold. After a strong year his ₹2,00,000 long-term money is ₹1,36,000 equity (68%), ₹56,000 debt (28%) and ₹8,000 gold (4%). Equity has drifted 8 points over. He sends his next six months of new investments entirely to debt, which brings him back near target without selling.

Rebalancing feels wrong: it means adding to what has done badly and slowing what has done well. That is exactly why it works: it makes you buy low and sell high by rule, not by feeling.

## Local example

**Anu** set her first allocation. Her short goals (emergency fund, course fees, two-wheeler) stay 100% safe in her savings account, RD and FDs. Her only long goal is retirement, starting small after Module 12.

For the retirement money, her risk profile came out **balanced**, so she wrote a target of **50% equity (through index funds, once she has studied them in Module 9), 45% debt (PPF), 5% gold**. Her rule: rebalance on 1 April each year if anything drifts more than 5 points, by sending new money to the lagging class first.

She noticed her family's wealth was mostly land and gold jewellery. She didn't try to change her parents' choices; she wrote, "My own new savings go to what our family doesn't have yet: insured deposits, PPF and, later, diversified equity."

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Principles of Finance on LibreTexts (CC BY 4.0)](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29) | Chapter 15, "How to Think about Investing": the sections on diversification and portfolios | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [NCFE: free basic financial education course (e-LMS, about 5 hours)](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430) | The long-term planning module (revision) with allocation in mind | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your own money)

1. In your Goals tab, add the target allocation for each goal's money using its horizon and your profile.
2. Make an **Allocation** tab with the template: list what you already hold (deposits, PPF, EPF, gold, any funds or shares), with asset class and value.
3. Enter your target percentages for long-term money and let the formulas show actual percentages and drift.
4. Write your rebalancing rule: date, drift limit, and "new money first".
5. Write one sentence on your biggest concentration risk and what you will do about it with new savings.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Allocation tab with targets, actuals and the drift formula, and your rebalancing rule, saved in 08 Basics.

## Template: Allocation tab

```
Holdings (rows 2-30): Holding,Asset class (Equity/Debt/Gold/Cash),Value (₹),For which goal
Summary (columns F-J):
F2: Equity   F3: Debt   F4: Gold   F5: Cash
G: actual value   G2: =SUMIF($B$2:$B$30,F2,$C$2:$C$30)   (copy to G3:G5)
H: actual %       H2: =IF(SUM($G$2:$G$5)>0,G2/SUM($G$2:$G$5)*100,0)
I: target %       (type: e.g. 60, 35, 5, 0)
J: drift          J2: =H2-I2
K: action         K2: =IF(ABS(J2)>5,IF(J2>0,"Over: send new money elsewhere","Under: send new money here"),"OK")
```

## Template: my rebalancing rule

```
I check my allocation every year on ____ (date).
If any asset class is more than ___ percentage points away from target, I rebalance.
First I send new money to the class below target. I sell only if that isn't enough, after checking tax and exit loads.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing funds before choosing an allocation.** Decide the split first; picking products comes after (Module 9).
- **Forgetting EPF, GPF and PPF.** They are debt. Count them, or you may hold more debt than you think.
- **Rebalancing too often.** Once a year with a drift limit is enough; frequent changes add costs and taxes.
- **Mistaking many products for diversification.** Five funds that hold the same companies aren't diversified. Look at what they own.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Money for a goal in 2 years should usually be…
    - A) Mostly in equity
    - B) All in safe options
    - C) In crypto
    - D) In one stock
2. Target 60% equity; actual 68%. With a 5-point rule, what do you do first?
    - A) Do nothing ever
    - B) Send new money to debt (and gold) until it is back near target
    - C) Buy more equity
    - D) Sell everything
3. Which is an example of diversification?
    - A) All savings in one co-op society
    - B) An index fund holding many companies, plus deposits and some gold
    - C) All savings in one company's shares
    - D) Five funds holding the same stocks
4. Your EPF balance belongs to which asset class?
    - A) Debt
    - B) Equity
    - C) Real estate
    - D) Gold

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax chapter 15 on diversification and the NCFE long-term planning module
- **Action:** Set target allocations, build the Allocation tab with drift formulas and write your rebalancing rule. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Allocation tab with targets, actuals and the drift formula, and your rebalancing rule, saved in 08 Basics.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** There is no time to recover from a fall.
2. **B.** Drift is 8 points; new money first avoids selling.
3. **B.** Spreading across and within asset classes reduces the damage from any one failure.
4. **A.** It earns a declared interest rate; count it as debt in your allocation.

sections.title: Final self-assessment and toolkit checklist
sections.summary: Retake the baseline self-assessment, compare your real money snapshot with your week 0 guesses, and check that every part of your plan exists.
sections.content:
Two things to finish the course: retake the baseline self-assessment, and check that every part of your plan exists.

## 1. Retake the self-assessment

Open the **Baseline** tab and fill in the **End** column for all 20 skills, without looking at your start scores first. Then compare:

- Which three skills grew the most? Write them in your one-page plan's notes.
- Any skill still at 1 or 2? Note which module covers it and plan one practice task for next month.
- Rewrite the **money snapshot** with real numbers now, next to your week 0 guesses. Where was your guess furthest from reality?

## 2. Check your toolkit

Each item should be a tab, a file or a note in your Money Folder that you could show a family member tomorrow. If something is missing, the module listed has its template.

| Toolkit item | Where the template is |
| --- | --- |
| Money Workbook with every tab filled in and dated | Week 0, used all course |
| Budget system: 30-day log, Budget tab with formulas, monthly routine | Module 3 |
| Net-worth tracker and cash-flow statement, updated this month | Module 2 |
| Emergency fund plan: target, where it is kept, monthly transfer, progress | Module 5 |
| Debt list with true costs, payoff plan and a checked credit report | Module 6 |
| Insurance checklist and a policy comparison done without buying | Module 7 |
| Investment Policy Statement, signed and dated | Modules 8, 9 and 17 |
| Tax checklist and the two-regime calculator | Module 10 |
| Goal funding plans and a retirement estimate | Modules 11 and 12 |
| Document register, nominations checked on every account, will decision | Module 13 |
| Scam-proof habits checklist, shared with your family | Module 15 |
| One-page financial plan and the yearly money-review checklist | Module 17 |

## Before you call the course done

- Save a backup of your progress from **Backup and courses** in this app, and keep it in your Money Folder.
- Download a copy of your Money Workbook (File → Download) and keep it offline too.
- Put your next monthly money date and your yearly review month in your calendar. The course ends; your money system doesn't.

sections.title: What next: your 12-month money routine
sections.summary: How to keep your money system running after the course: monthly, quarterly and yearly routines, life events, when to pay for advice and where to keep learning.
sections.content:
Finishing the course is the start of running your own money. Here is a sensible order for the next twelve months.

## Every month (30 minutes)

- The monthly money review on your money date: update the numbers, make one decision.
- Keep the 50/30/20 or zero-based budget you chose; log spending at least for one week each quarter, so you don't drift.

## Every quarter (1 hour)

- Small savings rates are announced every quarter: check if they changed ([India Post rates page](https://indiapost.gov.in/banking-services/saving)).
- Check your allocation against your Investment Policy Statement; rebalance only if it has drifted beyond your limits.
- Download your mutual fund and demat statement ([CAS](https://www.amfiindia.com/investor-corner/investor-center/cas.html)) and check that nominations and KYC show as complete.

## Every year (one weekend, in the same month every year)

Use the yearly money-review checklist from FIN-M17-L03: insurance renewals and cover, nominations, the will decision, the free credit reports, tax regime choice and ITR, goals and their timelines, and the one-page plan.

## When life changes, revisit these modules

| When this happens | Revisit |
| --- | --- |
| You get a Kerala government job | Module 14: the first-year plan, then Modules 7, 10 and 12 |
| You start freelancing or a business | FIN-M03-L04 and FIN-M10-L05, plus the Entrepreneurship course, Module 8 |
| Marriage or a child | Modules 7, 11 and 13: cover, goals and nominations |
| You plan to buy a house or vehicle | FIN-M11-L02 and FIN-M06-L03 |
| A big windfall: arrears, bonus, inheritance, sale of gold or land | Your Investment Policy Statement first, then Modules 8 and 9; wait 30 days before deciding |
| Someone offers a "great scheme" | Module 15, before you pay anything |

## When to pay for advice

You don't need an adviser to follow this course. Consider a fee-only SEBI-registered investment adviser when your investments become large or complicated, after a windfall, or before retirement. Check registration on the [SEBI list of registered investment advisers](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/other/OtherAction.do?doRecognisedFpi=yes&intmId=13) first, and read about fee limits in FIN-M09-L02. For tax notices or business accounts, use a chartered accountant.

## Keep learning, free

- [NCFE's free e-LMS course](https://ncfe.org.in/?p=430): about 5 hours on banking, insurance, pensions, investing and scams
- [Zerodha Varsity](https://zerodha.com/varsity/modules/): the Personal Finance, Mutual Funds, Insurance and NPS modules, read as education, not as product advice
- [OpenStax Principles of Finance](https://biz.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Finance/Principles_of_Finance_%28OpenStax%29): chapters 3, 7, 8, 15 and 20 for the theory behind interest, time value and risk
- [SEBI investor website](https://investor.sebi.gov.in/) and [RBI Financial Education](https://rbi.org.in/financialeducation/) for new rules and fraud warnings

## Keep up with rule changes

The Union Budget (usually on 1 February) can change tax rules; RBI changes rates through the year; Kerala announces DA and pay decisions by government order. Once a month, spend 15 minutes on the official pages linked in this course's sources log, and update your plan when something changes.

Every link on this page was checked on 2026-11-03; see the **Sources and verification log** for each one's status.

sections.title: Glossary with Malayalam meanings
sections.summary: 66 key personal finance terms in English and Malayalam, with simple meanings.
sections.content:
Key words from the course, roughly in the order you meet them. Many English words, such as EMI, SIP and KYC, are used as they are in Malayalam conversation; the Malayalam is given so you can explain them to family.

| English | മലയാളം (Malayalam) | Simple meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Budget** | ബജറ്റ് (വരവുചെലവ് പദ്ധതി) | A plan for how you will use the money you expect to receive |
| **Income** | വരുമാനം | Money you receive: salary, fees, business profit, interest |
| **Expense** | ചെലവ് | Money you spend |
| **Savings** | സമ്പാദ്യം | The part of income you don't spend |
| **Savings rate** | സമ്പാദ്യ നിരക്ക് | Savings as a percentage of income |
| **Needs and wants** | ആവശ്യങ്ങളും ആഗ്രഹങ്ങളും | What you must pay for, and what you would like to have |
| **Lifestyle inflation** | ജീവിതശൈലി ചെലവ് വർധന | Spending rising every time income rises, so saving never grows |
| **Asset** | ആസ്തി | Something you own that has money value |
| **Liability** | ബാധ്യത | Money you owe |
| **Net worth** | അറ്റ ആസ്തി | Everything you own minus everything you owe |
| **Cash flow** | പണമൊഴുക്ക് | Money coming in and going out over a period |
| **Emergency fund** | അടിയന്തര നിധി | Savings kept ready for job loss, illness or urgent repairs |
| **Inflation** | വിലക്കയറ്റം (പണപ്പെരുപ്പം) | Prices rising over time, so each rupee buys less |
| **Interest** | പലിശ | The price of borrowing money, or the reward for lending it |
| **Principal** | മുതൽ | The original amount borrowed or invested |
| **Compound interest** | കൂട്ടുപലിശ | Interest earned on earlier interest as well as on the principal |
| **EMI** | മാസത്തവണ (ഇ.എം.ഐ.) | Equated monthly instalment: a fixed monthly loan payment |
| **Loan** | വായ്പ | Money borrowed that must be repaid with interest |
| **Debt** | കടം | Money you owe to anyone |
| **Collateral** | ഈട് | Something pledged to a lender, such as gold, that can be taken if you don't repay |
| **Guarantor** | ജാമ്യക്കാരൻ | A person who promises to repay if the borrower doesn't |
| **Credit score** | ക്രെഡിറ്റ് സ്കോർ (വായ്പാ വിശ്വാസ്യത സ്കോർ) | A number that shows lenders how reliably you have repaid |
| **Savings account** | സേവിങ്സ് അക്കൗണ്ട് | A bank account for keeping money safely, with some interest |
| **Fixed deposit (FD)** | സ്ഥിര നിക്ഷേപം | A lump sum kept with a bank for a fixed time at a fixed rate |
| **Recurring deposit (RD)** | ആവർത്തന നിക്ഷേപം | A fixed amount deposited every month for a fixed time |
| **KYC** | ഉപഭോക്താവിനെ തിരിച്ചറിയൽ (കെ.വൈ.സി.) | Know Your Customer: proving your identity and address |
| **Nominee** | നോമിനി (നാമനിർദ്ദേശം ചെയ്യപ്പെട്ടയാൾ) | The person who receives the money in an account if you die |
| **Will** | വിൽപ്പത്രം | A written document saying who gets your property after you die |
| **Insurance** | ഇൻഷുറൻസ് | Paying a small, certain amount to be protected from a large, uncertain loss |
| **Premium** | പ്രീമിയം (ഇൻഷുറൻസ് തവണ) | The amount you pay for insurance |
| **Sum insured or sum assured** | ഇൻഷുറൻസ് തുക (പരിരക്ഷാ തുക) | The most the insurer will pay |
| **Claim** | ക്ലെയിം (നഷ്ടപരിഹാര അപേക്ഷ) | Asking the insurer to pay under your policy |
| **Term insurance** | ടേം ഇൻഷുറൻസ് (കാലാവധി ലൈഫ് ഇൻഷുറൻസ്) | Pure life cover for a fixed period, with no maturity payout |
| **Waiting period** | കാത്തിരിപ്പ് കാലയളവ് | Time after buying health cover before some illnesses are covered |
| **Investment** | നിക്ഷേപം | Putting money into something you expect to grow or pay income |
| **Risk** | നഷ്ടസാധ്യത (റിസ്ക്) | The chance that results differ from what you expect, including losses |
| **Return** | ആദായം (റിട്ടേൺ) | What an investment earns, as a percentage |
| **Real return** | യഥാർത്ഥ ആദായം | Return after subtracting inflation |
| **Asset allocation** | ആസ്തി വിന്യാസം | How your money is split between equity, debt, gold and cash |
| **Diversification** | വൈവിധ്യവൽക്കരണം | Spreading money across many investments so one failure hurts less |
| **Rebalancing** | പുനഃസന്തുലനം | Bringing your allocation back to its target |
| **Mutual fund** | മ്യൂച്വൽ ഫണ്ട് | A pool of many people's money invested by a professional manager |
| **SIP** | വ്യവസ്ഥാപിത നിക്ഷേപ പദ്ധതി (എസ്.ഐ.പി.) | Systematic investment plan: investing a fixed amount regularly |
| **NAV** | അറ്റ ആസ്തി മൂല്യം (എൻ.എ.വി.) | Net asset value: the price of one unit of a mutual fund |
| **Expense ratio** | ചെലവ് അനുപാതം | The yearly fee a fund takes, as a percentage of your money |
| **Index fund** | ഇൻഡക്സ് ഫണ്ട് (സൂചിക ഫണ്ട്) | A fund that simply copies a market index |
| **Share or stock** | ഓഹരി | A small part-ownership of a company |
| **Demat account** | ഡീമാറ്റ് അക്കൗണ്ട് | An account that holds shares and other securities electronically |
| **Dividend** | ലാഭവിഹിതം | Part of a company's or fund's profit paid to investors |
| **Capital gain** | മൂലധന നേട്ടം | Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid |
| **Income tax** | ആദായ നികുതി | Tax on your yearly income |
| **Tax regime** | നികുതി സമ്പ്രദായം | The set of rates and deductions you choose: old or new |
| **Deduction** | കിഴിവ് | An amount subtracted from income before tax is worked out |
| **TDS** | ഉറവിടത്തിൽ നികുതി പിടിക്കൽ (ടി.ഡി.എസ്.) | Tax deducted at source by the payer before paying you |
| **Income tax return (ITR)** | ആദായ നികുതി റിട്ടേൺ | The yearly statement of your income and tax filed with the department |
| **GST** | ചരക്ക് സേവന നികുതി (ജി.എസ്.ടി.) | Goods and Services Tax, charged on most sales of goods and services |
| **Provident fund** | പ്രൊവിഡന്റ് ഫണ്ട് (ഭാവിനിധി) | A long-term savings account for retirement, such as EPF, GPF or PPF |
| **Pension** | പെൻഷൻ | Regular income after retirement |
| **Dearness allowance (DA)** | ക്ഷാമബത്ത | An allowance added to pay to offset rising prices |
| **Retirement corpus** | വിരമിക്കൽ നിധി | The total savings you need to live on after you stop working |
| **Chitty** | ചിട്ടി (കുറി) | A group saving and borrowing scheme where members bid for the monthly prize |
| **Co-operative society** | സഹകരണ സംഘം | A member-owned organisation; some take deposits, but not all are licensed banks |
| **Ponzi scheme** | പോൻസി തട്ടിപ്പ് | A fraud that pays old investors with new investors' money until it collapses |
| **Phishing** | ഫിഷിങ് (വ്യാജ സന്ദേശ തട്ടിപ്പ്) | Fake messages or sites that trick you into giving passwords or OTPs |
| **Investment Policy Statement** | നിക്ഷേപ നയരേഖ | Your written rules for investing: goals, allocation, what you will and won't do |
| **Financial plan** | സാമ്പത്തിക പദ്ധതി | Your goals and the steps, numbers and dates to reach them |

sections.content:
Every link in this course is listed here with the date it was checked. Links were opened and read on 2026-11-03; nothing here was copied from memory. If a link stops working, search for its title on the same website.

- **verified 2026-11-03:** the page was opened on that date and its content matched what the course says.
- **verified 2026-11-03; check current rules:** as above, but it is a rate, limit or rule that changes often. Open the source before you act.
- **verified 2026-11-03 (headline checked):** the page could not be opened in full, so only its headline and date were checked in a web search. The course uses it only for what the headline itself says.
- **unverified:** the site blocks automated checks, so the page could not be opened for this course. The address is the official one named by other government sources; type it yourself and check that it is the real site.

Government and regulator pages are preferred. Where an official page could not be opened or doesn't exist in plain text, a dated news report or a bank's official page is used instead, and its date is in the title. OpenStax *Principles of Finance* is licensed CC BY 4.0, and this course only links to it.
